chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Muhammad ibn al-Haytham, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about the juice that is cooked by fire until it boils from its time, so its owner drinks it. He (peace be upon him) said: 'When it changes from its state and boils, there is no goodness in it until two-thirds of it disappears and one-third remains.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on cooked grape juice that boils and reduces in volume?
ai.summary: In *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the status of cooked grape juice (*asir*), ruling that once it boils and changes its state, it remains non-intoxicating or permissible until two-thirds evaporates, leaving one-third. This specific ratio highlights the Shia juristic principle that the transformation of the liquid's nature through concentration or boiling affects its legal classification, distinguishing it from fresh juice. The hadith serves as a foundational text for understanding the boundaries of *khamr* (intoxicant) in culinary and ritual contexts.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ibn Abu Najran, from Muhammad Bin Al Haysam, 
(It has been narrated) from a man from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, said,

‘I asked him<sup>asws</sup> about the (grape) juice cooked by the fire until it boils from a time, so its owner drinks it. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘When it changes from its (original) state and boils, so there is no goodness in it until two-thirds of it evaporates and there remains a third’.
en.sarwar: 2. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn abu Najran from Muhammad ibn al-Haytham from a man who has said the following:

“I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about grape juice which is cooked on fire until it boils for one hour; then the owner drinks it. He (the Imam) said, ‘If it changes and boils, it then becomes devoid of goodness until two-thirds of it is evaporated and only one-third has remained.’”
